title: If the Weather Is Good…
paragraphs: Kamila Seitkali loves making plans. Every Sunday evening she sits at her desk and writes in her notebook. She writes all her plans for the week. But she always adds one important word: 'if'.

'If the weather is good on Saturday, I will go to the park with Zhibek,' she writes. 'If I finish my essay by Thursday, I will watch a film on Friday. If I have enough money, I will buy new running shoes.'

Kamila's mother reads the notebook and smiles. 'You are very careful,' she says. 'You don't make promises — you make plans.' Kamila nods. 'If you make plans with conditions, you don't feel bad when things change,' she explains.

Amir Bekzhanov thinks differently. 'If the weather is good, I go outside immediately,' he tells Kamila. 'I don't wait. When the sun shines, I run. When it rains, I read. Simple rules for a simple life.' Kamila laughs. 'That's the zero conditional — no future, just facts!'

At WKU, students learn two types of conditionals in English class. The zero conditional talks about facts and general truths: 'If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.' The first conditional talks about real possibilities in the future: 'If I study hard, I will pass my exam.'

Dr. Akhmetov always says: 'Language and life are the same. In life, you use conditionals every day — when you plan, when you decide, when you dream. Learn them well, and English becomes your thinking tool.'

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Amir, what will you do if it rains this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I'll stay home and study. What about you?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: If it rains, I'll finish my English essay. If it's sunny, I'll go jogging.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Perfect plan. If we both finish our work, we can meet at the library on Sunday.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Deal! If the library is open, we will study together.
